lessons.title: Agents vs. Simple Chat
lessons.chapterTitle: What an AI Agent Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Take a real question that needs external info (e.g. 'what's the weather in the city with the most open support tickets right now') and write out both how a plain chat turn would have to guess at it and how a tool-equipped agent would work through it step by step.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side write-up contrasting the plain-chat guess against the agent's step-by-step approach for the same real question.

lessons.title: The Agent Loop: Plan, Act, Observe
lessons.chapterTitle: What an AI Agent Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own 3-iteration Plan/Act/Observe trace, in the style of the lesson's weather/tickets example, for a different real two-step question, then identify which of the 3 real stop conditions (model decides it's done, a hard limit, a human intervenes) would end it.
slots.deliverable: A written 3-iteration agent-loop trace plus the identified stop condition and why.

lessons.title: Tool Use Fundamentals
lessons.chapterTitle: What an AI Agent Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real tool definition (name, description, input_schema) of your own, then make a real call to the Claude Messages API with that tool and a matching user question, and capture the real tool_use block it returns.
slots.deliverable: Your tool definition JSON plus the real captured tool_use block from an actual API call.

lessons.title: Agent Frameworks, Overview
lessons.chapterTitle: What an AI Agent Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Compare the Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, and CrewAI against one real project idea you pick, writing one concrete trade-off for each framework on that specific project.
slots.deliverable: A written 3-framework comparison grounded in one specific project idea, with a final pick and justification.

lessons.title: When Agents Are Overkill
lessons.chapterTitle: What an AI Agent Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Take 3 real task descriptions (invent at least one) and sort each into 'single prompt,' 'fixed workflow,' or 'needs a real agent loop' using the lesson's one-question test, justifying each call.
slots.deliverable: A written classification of 3 tasks with justification for each category.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite the lesson's 'poor' get_stock_price description from memory so it meets all 4 self-review checklist items, then write one new real tool schema of your own and run it through the same checklist.
slots.deliverable: The rewritten get_stock_price description plus one original tool schema that passes the 4-item checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Make a real two-turn Messages API exchange (tool_use then tool_result) using tool_choice: {"type": "auto"} for a tool of your choice, then repeat the same call forcing it with tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": ...} and note the real difference in Claude's narration text.
slots.deliverable: Both real API exchanges captured side by side, annotated with the observed tool_choice difference.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 real tool_result error payloads for the same failed tool call — one using a vague 'failed' message and one using an instructive message per the lesson's guidance — then send the instructive version to a real Claude API call and observe how it adapts its next response.
slots.deliverable: The vague vs. instructive tool_result pair plus Claude's real captured response to the instructive version.

slots.practicalActivity: Take 6 near-duplicate tool ideas you invent (e.g. create_pr/review_pr/merge_pr plus 3 more) and consolidate them into 2 tools with an action parameter and clear service namespacing, following the lesson's routing guidance.
slots.deliverable: The original 6 ambiguous tool names plus your consolidated, namespaced 2-tool redesign.

slots.practicalActivity: Send a real Messages API request with 2 independent tools available (e.g. get_weather and get_traffic) for a question needing both, capture the real multi-block tool_use response, and send back both tool_result blocks correctly matched by tool_use_id.
slots.deliverable: The real captured multi-tool_use response plus your correctly matched tool_result reply.

slots.practicalActivity: Call a real public API that returns a large JSON blob (a weather or stock API works well), then write the high-signal, trimmed tool_result string you'd actually return to the model instead of the raw payload.
slots.deliverable: The raw real API response alongside your trimmed, high-signal tool_result string.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter wrap lab: build a real 2-tool agent loop from scratch against the Messages API (no framework), with well-designed schemas, instructive error handling, and correctly matched multi-tool tool_result formatting, then run it end to end on a real multi-step question.
slots.deliverable: A working script implementing a real multi-tool agent loop with captured real output for an end-to-end test question.

lessons.title: What MCP Is & Why It Exists

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real product or service you use and sketch what its own MCP server's tool list might look like (names plus one-line descriptions), then explain in writing why building it once beats a custom integration per AI app, using the lesson's M x N framing.
slots.deliverable: A written sketch of a real MCP server's tools plus the M x N explanation.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram host/client/server for a scenario where one host connects to 2 real MCP servers at once (e.g. a filesystem server and the Sentry server), labeling which transport — stdio or Streamable HTTP — each connection would use.
slots.deliverable: A labeled host/client/server diagram for a real 2-server scenario with transport types identified.

slots.practicalActivity: Take 3 real feature ideas (e.g. 'check inventory levels,' 'read a calendar,' 'run a saved vacation-planning template') and correctly classify each as an MCP tool, resource, or prompt, justifying who controls each one.
slots.deliverable: A written classification of 3 features into tool/resource/prompt with justification for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Install the real MCP Python SDK (uv add "mcp[cli]") and build a simple stdio MCP server exposing 1-2 real tools with type-hinted, docstring-documented functions, using the logging module (never print) for any diagnostic output.
slots.deliverable: A working local MCP server file with 1-2 real tools, verified to run without stdout corruption.

lessons.title: Connecting an Agent to an MCP Server

slots.practicalActivity: Configure Claude Desktop's claude_desktop_config.json to launch your own server from the previous slot (or the official Filesystem Server), confirm its tools appear after the real discovery handshake, and run one real tool call through it with approval.
slots.deliverable: Your real claude_desktop_config.json entry plus a captured log or screenshot of the connected server's discovered tools and one successful real tool call.

slots.practicalActivity: Take 3 real tool ideas — one genuinely one-off, one multiple teams would want, and one a reference server probably already covers — and apply the lesson's 3-question framework to decide build-custom vs. build-MCP vs. connect-to-existing for each.
slots.deliverable: A written decision table for the 3 tool ideas with the right approach and reasoning for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own full ReAct-style trace (Thought/Action/Observation, 3 iterations) for a real two-lookup question of your choosing, then remove the Thought lines and explain specifically what becomes harder to debug without them.
slots.deliverable: The full annotated ReAct trace plus a written explanation of what breaks without the Thought steps.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real upfront plan (ordered steps) for a multi-part goal you choose, then force one step to fail partway through and show how you'd replan just that one step without discarding the rest of the plan.
slots.deliverable: The original plan, the forced failure, and the revised plan showing only the one step replaced.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a real 3-agent split (research/writer/reviewer, each with a narrow tool set and role) for a task you choose, specifying exactly what each agent's context does and doesn't see.
slots.deliverable: A written 3-agent design specifying each agent's role, tools, and context boundaries.

slots.practicalActivity: Design an orchestrator/worker breakdown for 2 different real inputs to the same goal (e.g. two different competitor announcements, one mentioning pricing and one not), showing the dynamic worker count genuinely differs between them.
slots.deliverable: Two worked orchestrator/worker breakdowns for the same goal type, showing a different number of workers spawned for each real input.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real generate-then-evaluate trace (the evaluator-optimizer pattern) where a first draft summary is deliberately wrong, the evaluator catches a specific omission against the real source text, and a revised draft fixes it.
slots.deliverable: The draft/evaluate/revise trace with the specific caught error and the corrected final output.

slots.practicalActivity: Take a long-running agent scenario from an earlier slot in this chapter and decide which of the 3 memory mechanisms (conversation history, scratchpad, external memory) fits its accumulated state best, then write one example scratchpad summary condensing that state.
slots.deliverable: A written mechanism choice with justification plus one example condensed scratchpad summary.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter wrap lab: pick one real multi-step goal and build it two ways — a simple reactive loop and an orchestrator/worker design with at least 2 real workers — then compare which one actually produced a better-organized result and why.
slots.deliverable: Two working implementations (reactive vs. orchestrator/worker) of the same real goal with a written comparison of their outputs.

slots.practicalActivity: Take 2 real tool names you invent (one like update_ticket_priority, one like issue_refund) and apply the lesson's 3-part rule of thumb — irreversible, costly, low-confidence — to decide which one needs a human-approval checkpoint.
slots.deliverable: A written decision for both tools using the 3-part rule of thumb, with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Construct a real consequential tool_use block yourself (tool name, exact arguments, the agent's stated reasoning, and the real concrete effect), design the approval-checkpoint display for it, then write both the approved and rejected real tool_result payloads.
slots.deliverable: Your constructed tool_use block, the approval-checkpoint display content, and both approved and rejected tool_result payloads.

slots.practicalActivity: Design all 3 escalation patterns (timeout, tiered, fallback-to-safe) for a real tool call you choose, then pick which pattern actually fits that tool's risk profile and justify ruling out the other two.
slots.deliverable: A written escalation design applying the one best-fitting pattern to a real tool, with the other two patterns ruled out and why.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real audit log entry (in the lesson's JSON shape) for an approved tool call and a second entry for a rejected one, then explain in writing why both need to be kept, not just the successful one.
slots.deliverable: Two real audit log entries (approved and rejected) with a written justification for logging both.

slots.practicalActivity: Classify 3 real tool ideas you choose into the lesson's 3 undo categories (true reversal, compensating action, can't undo/contain), and for each, write out concretely what 'fixing a mistake' would actually look like.
slots.deliverable: A written classification of 3 tools into undo categories with a concrete fix-it plan for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Set the 3 real limits (MAX_ITERATIONS, MAX_WALL_CLOCK, MAX_REPEAT_CALLS) for an agent scenario you design, then construct a realistic runaway trace and identify which specific limit would catch it and why the other two wouldn't.
slots.deliverable: Your 3 configured limits plus a written runaway scenario showing which limit catches it and why.

slots.practicalActivity: Using real Claude API usage/pricing numbers, calculate a per-task cost budget for a scenario you choose, set a matching action-scope limit (records modified, distinct tools, external calls), and show the real arithmetic for exactly when the budget would trip.
slots.deliverable: A worked cost-budget calculation plus a defined action-scope limit for your chosen task scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Write down a realistic over-broad API key/scope for an agent, then redesign it into a least-privilege scoped credential matching only the specific tools your agent scenario actually needs, plus a sandbox config (network allowlist, filesystem access) for any code-execution tool.
slots.deliverable: The before (over-broad) and after (scoped) credential definitions plus a written sandbox configuration.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real adversarial tool_result (an embedded 'ignore previous instructions' attempt) the unmitigated way, then rewrite it using the lesson's real JSON-encoding mitigation, and check your rewrite against the 6-item defensive checklist.
slots.deliverable: The before/after tool_result pair (plain text vs. JSON-encoded) plus a completed 6-item checklist review.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a simple monitoring dashboard tracking the lesson's 4 real signals (rejection rate, limit-trip frequency, injection flags, cost trend) for an agent you specify, then write a realistic drift scenario (e.g. rejection rate climbing from 5% to 35%) and name 2 distinct root causes it could point to.
slots.deliverable: A written 4-signal monitoring design plus a drift scenario with 2 distinct root-cause hypotheses.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the capstone's real done-checklist (get_order/issue_refund schemas, an approval checkpoint, audit logging, stopping conditions, a budget, scoped credentials) as your own project plan, and explain in writing why get_order doesn't need an approval checkpoint but issue_refund does.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone project plan using the real done-checklist plus the get_order vs. issue_refund reasoning.

lessons.title: Capstone: Building a Tool-Using Agent With Human Approval

slots.practicalActivity: Build the real get_order and issue_refund tool schemas and the approval-checkpoint-gated handle_tool_use function from the lesson, then run a real end-to-end round trip: a refund request, a human approval, and a resumed loop confirming the refund.
slots.deliverable: Working code for both tools and the gated handler, plus a captured real end-to-end approved-refund transcript.

slots.practicalActivity: Wrap your Lesson-35 agent with an audit log entry per call, task-specific stopping conditions and budget (MAX_ITERATIONS=8, budget_usd=0.50, MAX_RECORDS_MODIFIED=1), and a least-privilege scoped credential, without touching the existing tool or approval logic.
slots.deliverable: The wrapped agent code with real audit log output and a demonstrated budget or iteration limit actually tripping in a test run.

slots.practicalActivity: Run your capstone agent against the lesson's real 6-item pre-deployment checklist, fixing at least the audit-log-to-durable-storage and config-driven-limits items, and write out your defined behavior for 'approver didn't respond.'
slots.deliverable: A completed 6-item deployment checklist with at least 2 real fixes applied, plus a written no-response escalation policy.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the capstone's portfolio README covering the architecture, a demonstrated rejection path, a tripped stopping condition, and a real audit log entry, then rehearse explaining the project's 'sentence that ties it together' out loud.
slots.deliverable: A README.md portfolio writeup containing the real demonstrated rejection, limit-trip, and audit-log evidence from the capstone.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design and build a real tool-using AI agent — writing good tool schemas, connecting to MCP servers, choosing the right architecture (ReAct, planning, multi-agent, orchestrator/worker), and wrapping it in human-approval checkpoints, audit logging, cost and action limits, sandboxing, and injection defenses — culminating in a deployable refund agent with every safety control actually verified working.
